search_documents.text: Winning-ticket initializations discovered by iterative magnitude pruning on large, complex natural-image source datasets produce sparse initializations that, when used to train a VGG19 or ResNet50 architecture on other natural-image target datasets, frequently achieve test accuracies on the target tasks that are close to the accuracies obtained by winning tickets discovered directly on those target datasets.
search_documents.title: claim_1

search_documents.text: The transferability described in claim 1 is observed across a wide range of pruning fractions.
search_documents.title: claim_2

search_documents.text: Larger / more class-rich source datasets produced stronger cross-dataset transfer than smaller sources.
search_documents.title: claim_3

search_documents.text: CIFAR-100 tickets generalize better than CIFAR-10 tickets despite both having 50,000 training examples.
search_documents.title: claim_4

search_documents.text: Winning tickets discovered on larger source datasets—both in terms of number of training examples and number of output classes—transfer substantially better to other natural-image classification datasets than tickets discovered on smaller source datasets, for both VGG19 and ResNet50 architectures.
search_documents.title: claim_5

search_documents.text: The effect described in claim 5, whereby winning tickets discovered on larger source datasets transfer substantially better to other natural-image classification datasets than tickets discovered on smaller source datasets, is not solely explained by raw training-set size.
search_documents.title: claim_6

search_documents.text: Holding training-set size fixed, a source dataset with many classes produced tickets that generalized better across targets than one with few classes.
search_documents.title: claim_7

search_documents.text: Winning-ticket initializations generated with one optimizer generalize to training with a different optimizer on natural-image classification datasets.
search_documents.title: claim_8

search_documents.text: VGG19 tickets found using SGD with momentum or using Adam, when re-used with the alternate optimizer, achieve high performance that is comparable to tickets discovered under the target optimizer.
search_documents.title: claim_9

search_documents.text: There are optimizer-dependent nuances in behavior in the transfer described in claim 8.
search_documents.title: claim_10

search_documents.text: Tickets transferred from SGD to Adam sometimes under-perform random tickets at low pruning fractions but outperform random tickets at high pruning fractions.
search_documents.title: claim_11

search_documents.text: A winning ticket discovered on CIFAR-10a (a subset of the CIFAR-10 dataset containing 25,000 training images with 2,500 images per class), transfers to a disjoint subset CIFAR-10b from the same data distribution and improves training on that held-out subset relative to random sparse initializations.
search_documents.title: claim_12

search_documents.text: The within-distribution transfer described in claim 12 holds for both VGG19 and ResNet50.
search_documents.title: claim_13

search_documents.text: ResNet50 showed sensitivity at low pruning fractions, occasionally under-performing random tickets when few weights are pruned.
search_documents.title: claim_14

search_documents.text: When performing magnitude pruning for winning-ticket discovery on VGG19 trained on CIFAR-10, globally ranking weights across all layers and pruning the smallest-magnitude weights globally yields higher-performing sparse subnetworks than pruning a fixed fraction per layer.
search_documents.title: claim_15

search_documents.text: Under global magnitude pruning the pruning fractions vary across layers: deeper convolutional layers are pruned more heavily while early layers retain a much larger fraction of their parameters.
search_documents.title: claim_16

search_documents.text: For VGG19 trained on CIFAR-10, the structure of the pruning mask contains substantial information useful for training sparse networks.
search_documents.title: claim_17

search_documents.text: Comparing (a) preserved winning-ticket masks, (b) masks permuted only within layers (local permutation), and (c) masks permuted across all layers (global permutation) shows that locally permuting a mask degrades performance moderately while globally permuting the mask degrades performance dramatically.
search_documents.title: claim_18

search_documents.text: A fair "random ticket" baseline for evaluating a winning-ticket initialization should randomize both weight values and mask structure (global permutation).
search_documents.title: claim_19

search_documents.text: For obtaining competitive winning tickets in the large-model and large-dataset regime of natural-image classification, an iterative magnitude-pruning schedule with pruning fraction per iteration 0.2 (20% of remaining parameters) over up to 30 iterations combined with late resetting to parameters at a small early training iteration—resetting to the parameters after 1 epoch for Fashion-MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and after 3 epochs for ImageNet and Places365—produced effective winning tickets, with learning-rate annealing schedules and other hyperparameters matched per model family.
search_documents.title: claim_20

search_documents.text: Winning-ticket initializations discovered by iterative magnitude pruning on ImageNet, Places365, and, to a lesser extent, CIFAR-100 produce sparse initializations that, when used to train a VGG19 or ResNet50 architecture on SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and Places365, frequently achieve test accuracies on the target tasks that are close to the accuracies obtained by winning tickets discovered directly on those target datasets.
search_documents.title: claim_21

search_documents.text: The transferability described in claim 1 is observed across a wide range of pruning fractions, including very high sparsity.
search_documents.title: claim_22

search_documents.text: Winning tickets discovered on larger source datasets—both in terms of number of training examples and number of output classes—transfer substantially better to SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and Places365 than tickets discovered on smaller source datasets, for both VGG19 and ResNet50 architectures.
search_documents.title: claim_23

search_documents.text: Holding training-set size fixed, CIFAR-100, a source dataset with 100 classes, produced tickets that generalized better across targets than CIFAR-10, a source dataset with 10 classes.
search_documents.title: claim_24

search_documents.text: Under global magnitude pruning the pruning fractions vary across layers: deeper convolutional layers are pruned more heavily while the first convolutional layer retains a much larger fraction of its parameters.
